chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad ibn Usman, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the child steals, he is excused (from cutting the hand). If he repeats, he is rebuked (with a light punishment). If he repeats, the ends of the fingers are cut. If he repeats, he is cut lower than that.

And he (peace be upon him) said: 'A boy was brought to Ali (peace be upon him) with doubt regarding whether he had reached the age of sexual maturity (had bed-wetted), so he cut the ends of the fingers.'

key_terms.احْتِلَامٌ: Sexual maturity (indicated by wet dream or bed-wetting)

ai.seo_question: What is the graduated penalty for a child who commits theft according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the graduated penal system for juvenile theft, reflecting the Shia juristic principle of balancing deterrence with the mitigation of liability for those lacking full legal maturity (bulugh). The progression from exemption to fingertip amputation and finally to lower hand amputation demonstrates a calibrated approach where the severity of the physical penalty increases with the frequency of recidivism, while the accompanying narration regarding the doubtful case of Ali ibn Abi Talib highlights the application of these rules in practical judicial contexts.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad Bin Usman, from Al Halby, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘When the child steals, he would be excused from it. So if he repeats, he is rebuked. So if he repeats, the ends of the fingers are cut. So if he repeats, he would be cut lower than that’.
And he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘They came to Ali<sup>asws</sup> with a boy, there was doubt with regards to him having bed-wetted yet. So he<sup>asws</sup> cut the ends of the fingers’.
